tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
- **By clang's reading, not by spelling.** BR-13 already reads each
  compile line's CPU and features from clang's own `-###` line
  (`note_cpu`, now `read_cpu` and `note_cpu`). The check takes the same
  reading of every folder file's flags (the base's for its kind, then
  its folders'), so `-mcpu=r4`, `-mfprev2`, `-msimd`, a
  `-target-feature` and a flag the toolchain gains later are caught
  alike. The toolchain's target knows CPUs `generic` and `r1` to `r5`
  with variants (`r3s`, `r3v1`, ...), and nine features, among them
  `fprev1` (float), `fprev2` (float and double) and `simd` (its
  `-mcpu=help`).
- **What passes.** CPU exactly `r3` (not `r3s` or another variant), and
  of the features, each taken at its last `+` or `-`, none enabled but
  `fprev1`. So the base's own set, `-mfprev1` again, and
  `-mno-fprev1` (no float instructions: soft-float, which the base's
  runtime provides) all pass; the face-value reading of "+fprev1 or
  none". A reading with no CPU (clang read none) is refused too.
- **Where.** Only `--src` folders' files that have folder flags: the
  base's own files keep the base's flags, and two of the base's builds
  read without a CPU on purpose (the runtime's C and the Plaits demo,
  which are soft-float; the demo's `PLAITS_HWFLOAT` build adds `+fprev1`
  through `-Xclang -target-feature`, the SDK's set, and stays as it is).
- **When.** Every folder file is checked before any is compiled, so the
  refusal comes before a compiler error and once per option, folder and
  effect ("and N more" files), on stderr only. The message names the
  option and the folder whose own flags give the effect, as the user
  gave them (carried into the container beside the mount path; only
  messages see it, so the outputs stay the same from any place; every
  folder of the file, if only their flags together give it), the first
  file, what the flag does, which of the folder's flags alone give it
  and the fix.
- **`-Xclang`.** The owner named `-Xclang -target-feature` among the
  spellings to catch. A folder can't give it: `check_flags` takes only
  the listed families, and `-Xclang` is not one (refused at exit 2
  since clean-1028). The reading would catch it if it ever got through;
  its reading (`+fprev2`, the same as `-mfprev2`'s) is in the unit test.
  Through `-m`, `-mllvm` passes options to the code generator, past
  the driver's reading; `-mllvm -mattr=...` and `-mllvm -mcpu=...` are
  not options this toolchain knows (it stops on them), so it is no
  route today, but it is the one the reading doesn't see.
- **Tested.** C-UNIT (`tests/test_build_flags.py`): the verdict on the
  readings of the SDK's set, `-mcpu=r3` alone, `-mno-fprev1`, another
  CPU, no CPU, double precision, SIMD and an unlisted feature. C-SEAMS
  (case flags): the flags folder built with `-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1`,
  `-mno-fprev1` (inner/, read as without float instructions), C++
  `-mfprev1` and assembly `-mcpu=r3`; and refused, each before any of
  its files is compiled, with its message: inner/ `-mcpu=r4`, the C++
  `-O2 -mfprev2` (only `-mfprev2` named) and the assembly `-msimd`.

content.content:
# base's own, to every C file under DIR, a --src folder or a folder in
# one; --cxxflags to its C++, --asflags to its assembly. Repeatable; a
# file under several such folders gets each one's flags in the order
# given (so a folder inside another can override it, -O2 after -O0, say).
# The base's own files, its runtime included, are always built with the
# base's flags. FLAGS are words of A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and _ = + . , / : -;
# a relative path in -I, -isystem or -iquote (joined to it: -Iinclude)
# is from DIR. Only these families are taken: -D, -U, -O, -W, -w, -f,
# -m, -std=, -I, -isystem, -iquote, -g, -pedantic, -ansi; and of them
# not those that would reach the host, the outputs' determinism or
# another tool: an absolute path or one with "..", -fdebug-prefix-map
# and its kin, -fprofile..., -fplugin..., -fpass-plugin...,
# -fsave-optimization-record, -Wa, -Wp, -Wl (check_flags). And since
# clean-pin-flags (amending BR-11) a folder's objects are built for the
# SDK's CPU and float, whatever its -m flags: clang's reading of each
# file's flags (read_cpu, BR-13's) must give CPU r3 and of the features
# fprev1 or none (check_cpu), or the build stops before compiling any of
# the folder's files, naming the folder, what the flag does and the fix.
#
# The platform (BR-2): --platform leaves out the base's instrument, the
# files below, defines SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL (firmware/src/engine.h) and
# links with firmware/platform.ld, whose assertions cover only the
# platform's records; --ld SCRIPT links with a script of one's own
# instead (in the base or in a --src folder), which includes platform.ld
# (INCLUDE platform.ld) and asserts its own records.
set -eu

INSTRUMENT="firmware/src/arp.c firmware/src/fm.c firmware/src/fm_play.c
            firmware/src/patches.c firmware/src/saving.c firmware/src/spectrum.c firmware/src/views.c"

ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
PLATFORM=linux/amd64

sha256() {
    if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then sha256sum "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1
    else shasum -a 256 "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1; fi
}

image_tag() {
    echo "small-beeps-build:$(sha256 "$ROOT/tools/Dockerfile" | cut -c1-16)"
}

cmd_image() {
    # No build context: the Dockerfile fetches everything it needs.
    docker build --platform "$PLATFORM" -t "$(image_tag)" - < "$ROOT/tools/Dockerfile"
    docker image inspect --format 'image {{.Id}}' "$(image_tag)"
}

# Refuses per-folder flags (BR-11) that could reach the host, make the
# outputs depend on where things are, or undo the build: only the
# families below are taken (above).
check_flags() {
    case "$2" in
        *[!A-Za-z0-9_=+.,/:\ -]*) echo "build: $1 '$2': flags are words of A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and _ = + . , / : -" >&2; exit 2 ;;
    esac
    for w in $2; do
        case "$w" in
            /*|*=/*|-I/*|-isystem/*|-iquote/*|*..*)
                echo "build: $1 '$w': no absolute paths or .. (a path is from the folder)" >&2; exit 2 ;;
            -fdebug-prefix-map=*|-ffile-prefix-map=*|-fmacro-prefix-map=*|-fcoverage-prefix-map=*| \
            -fprofile*|-fplugin*|-fpass-plugin*|-fsave-optimization-record*|-Wa,*|-Wp,*|-Wl,*)
                echo "build: $1 '$w' is not one a folder may set" >&2; exit 2 ;;
            -D?*|-U?*|-O|-O?|-W?*|-w|-f?*|-m?*|-std=?*|-I?*|-isystem?*|-iquote?*|-g|-g0|-g1|-g2|-g3| \
            -pedantic|-pedantic-errors|-ansi) ;;
            *) echo "build: $1 '$w' is not one a folder may set (-D, -U, -O, -W, -w, -f, -m, -std=, -I, -isystem, -iquote, -g, -pedantic, -ansi)" >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
}

cmd_build() {
    out="" src_mount=/mnt/small-beeps-src defines="" demo="" mounts="" srcs="" leave="" n=0
    platform="" ldscript="" ff="" srcnames=""
    while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
        case "$1" in
            --out) out=$2; shift 2 ;;

# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
import os
import re
import subprocess
import unittest

from tests.helpers import ROOT


class BuildFlagsTest(unittest.TestCase):
    """Requirements: R-BUILD-1"""

    def setUp(self):
        with open(os.path.join(ROOT, "tools", "build.sh"), encoding="utf-8") as f:
            self.script = f.read()

    def test_the_chips_cpu_model_and_float_instructions(self):
        # HW-62: the SDK builds for this CPU model with fprev1.
        m = re.search(r'^\s*CPU="([^"]*)"', self.script, re.M)
        self.assertIsNotNone(m)
        self.assertEqual(m.group(1).split(), ["-mcpu=r3", "-mfprev1"])

    def test_c_and_assembly_both_use_it(self):
        for name in ("CFLAGS", "ASFLAGS"):
            m = re.search(r'^\s*%s="-target pi32v2 \$CPU ' % name, self.script, re.M)
            self.assertIsNotNone(m, name)


class FolderCpuTest(unittest.TestCase):
    """Requirements: R-BUILD-5

    A --src folder's objects are built for the SDK's CPU and float
    (clean-pin-flags): tools/build.sh's cpu_effects, on readings as
    read_cpu makes them from clang's -### line (the build image's clang
    gives these for the flags named)."""

    def setUp(self):
        with open(os.path.join(ROOT, "tools", "build.sh"), encoding="utf-8") as f:
            m = re.search(r"^cpu_effects\(\) \{\n.*?^\}\n", f.read(), re.M | re.S)
        self.assertIsNotNone(m)
        self.func = m.group(0)

    def effects(self, reading):
        out = subprocess.run(["sh", "-c", self.func + 'cpu_effects "$1"', "sh", reading],
                             check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
        return out.splitlines()

    def test_the_sdks_set_and_none_pass(self):
        for reading in (" -mcpu=r3 -mattr=+fprev1",           # the base's flags, and -mfprev1 again
                        " -mcpu=r3",                          # -mcpu=r3 alone
                        " -mcpu=r3 -mattr=-fprev1",           # -mno-fprev1
                        " -mcpu=r3 -mattr=+fprev1,+fprev2,-fprev2"):
            self.assertEqual(self.effects(reading), [], reading)

    def test_another_cpu(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.effects(" -mcpu=r4 -mattr=+fprev1"), ["another CPU, r4 (the SDK's is r3)"])
        self.assertEqual(self.effects(" -mcpu=r3s -mattr=+fprev1"), ["another CPU, r3s (the SDK's is r3)"])
        self.assertEqual(self.effects(""), ["no particular CPU (clang read none from the flags; the SDK's is r3)"])

## 5. Build

```sh
sh base/tools/build.sh build --out out --platform --src src --ld src/my.ld
```

| Option | What |
|--------|------|
| `--platform` | leaves out the base's instrument (its FM engine, presets, arpeggiator, screens and saving), builds with `SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL`, links with `platform.ld` |
| `--src DIR` | every `.c`, `.S` and `.cc` under DIR, built with the firmware's flags and `-I DIR`; repeat it for more folders (not a folder holding `base/`) |
| `--ld SCRIPT` | your linker script (in `base/` or in a `--src` folder) |
| `--define NAME` | `-DNAME` for every source (yours and the base's) |
| `--leave-out FILE` | a base source left out (`firmware/src/...`), to replace it with your own |
| `--cflags DIR FLAGS` | FLAGS for the C files under DIR (a `--src` folder or a folder inside one), after the firmware's flags; the base's own files never get them |
| `--cxxflags DIR FLAGS` | the same for the C++ (`.cc`) files under DIR |
| `--asflags DIR FLAGS` | the same for the assembly (`.S`) files under DIR |

**Flags for your own folders.** Your code can have flags of its own, folder
by folder, while the base's files keep the base's (R-BUILD-5):

```sh
sh base/tools/build.sh build --out out --platform --src src --ld src/my.ld \
    --cflags src "-DMY_BOARD=2 -Wno-sign-compare" \
    --cflags src/vendor/dsp "-O2 -w -Iinclude" \
    --cxxflags src "-std=c++17"
```

- A file gets the flags of every folder it is under, in the order you
  gave them, after the firmware's own (so `-O2` here replaces the
  firmware's `-Os` for `src/vendor/dsp`, and its `-w` silences the
  warnings the firmware's `-Werror` would stop on).
- `--cflags` is for `.c` files only, `--cxxflags` for `.cc`, `--asflags`
  for `.S` (which are run through the preprocessor, so `-D` works there).
- A path in `-I`, `-isystem` or `-iquote` is from the folder the flags are
  for, and is joined to it: `-Iinclude`, not `-I include`.
- Taken: `-D`, `-U`, `-O`, `-W`, `-w`, `-f`, `-m`, `-std=`, `-I`,
  `-isystem`, `-iquote`, `-g`, `-pedantic`, `-ansi`, as words of letters,
  digits and `_ = + . , / : -`. Refused, so the build stays deterministic
  and inside its container: absolute paths and `..`, `-fdebug-prefix-map`
  and its kin, `-fprofile...`, `-fplugin...`, `-Wa,`, `-Wp,`, `-Wl,`,
  and anything else (`-o`, `-c`, `-x`, `-include`, `-target`, `@file`, ...).
- Your code is built for the SDK's CPU and float, whatever its flags:
  CPU r3, with the chip's single-precision float instructions (`fprev1`,
  as the base is built) or without float instructions (`-mno-fprev1`).
  Other `-m` flags are yours. The build reads each file's flags as the
  compiler does (its `-###` reading, the same the write-back check uses),
  so `-mcpu=`, `-mfprev2`, `-msimd`, a `-target-feature` and any flag
  with the same effect are all caught, and it stops before compiling any
  of your files, naming the folder, what the flag does and the fix:

  ```
  build: --cxxflags src: src/dsp/fir.cc would be built for double-precision float (fprev2), which the SDK's flags exclude and fwtest doesn't run (from -mfprev2).
  build:   Fix: take that out of --cxxflags src. Every --src folder is built for the SDK's CPU, r3, with its single-precision float (fprev1, as the base is) or without float instructions (-mno-fprev1); other -m flags are yours to set (BR-11; docs/BUILDING-ON-SMALL-BEEPS.md, section 5).
  FAIL: a folder's flags build for another CPU or other features than the SDK's (above)
  ```

  Refused alike: another CPU (`-mcpu=r4`, even `r3s`), SIMD (`-msimd`),
  and any other feature the toolchain has. fwtest
  runs what the SDK's flags give (R-HARN-14), not these.
- `--define NAME` stays the way to set something for every file, the
  base's included.

The outputs, in `out/`:

- `app.bin`: the raw image (linked at `0x02000000`), what fwtest and the
  app run;
- `app-pkg.bin`: the same code linked at `0x02000120`, for a `.fwsc`
  package (section 6);
- `app.elf`, `app-pkg.elf`: with symbols, for finding things;
- `app.size`: code, data, RAM and stack in bytes;
- `SHA256SUMS`.

The build is deterministic: the same sources give the same bytes, from
any folder on any machine. It refuses an object holding a store that
writes back into its own base register (`[++rN=k] = rN`, ...), as what
the chip does then is still open (R-BUILD-3); if your code trips it, the
message names the file, the function and the instruction. It reads each
object as it was compiled, with the CPU and float features your flags
gave it (`-mfprev1`, or a folder's own `-m` flags), and it refuses code
it can't read at all (`unreadable`), rather than guess past it.

class FolderCpuTest(unittest.TestCase):
    """Requirements: R-BUILD-5

    A --src folder's objects are built for the SDK's CPU and float
    (clean-pin-flags): tools/build.sh's cpu_effects, on readings as
    read_cpu makes them from clang's -### line (the build image's clang
    gives these for the flags named)."""

    def setUp(self):
        with open(os.path.join(ROOT, "tools", "build.sh"), encoding="utf-8") as f:
            m = re.search(r"^cpu_effects\(\) \{\n.*?^\}\n", f.read(), re.M | re.S)
        self.assertIsNotNone(m)
        self.func = m.group(0)

    def effects(self, reading):
        out = subprocess.run(["sh", "-c", self.func + 'cpu_effects "$1"', "sh", reading],
                             check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
        return out.splitlines()

    def test_the_sdks_set_and_none_pass(self):
        for reading in (" -mcpu=r3 -mattr=+fprev1",           # the base's flags, and -mfprev1 again
                        " -mcpu=r3",                          # -mcpu=r3 alone
                        " -mcpu=r3 -mattr=-fprev1",           # -mno-fprev1
                        " -mcpu=r3 -mattr=+fprev1,+fprev2,-fprev2"):
            self.assertEqual(self.effects(reading), [], reading)

    def test_another_cpu(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.effects(" -mcpu=r4 -mattr=+fprev1"), ["another CPU, r4 (the SDK's is r3)"])
        self.assertEqual(self.effects(" -mcpu=r3s -mattr=+fprev1"), ["another CPU, r3s (the SDK's is r3)"])
        self.assertEqual(self.effects(""), ["no particular CPU (clang read none from the flags; the SDK's is r3)"])

## 5. Build

```sh
sh base/tools/build.sh build --out out --platform --src src --ld src/my.ld
```

| Option | What |
|--------|------|
| `--platform` | leaves out the base's instrument (its FM engine, presets, arpeggiator, screens and saving), builds with `SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL`, links with `platform.ld` |
| `--src DIR` | every `.c`, `.S` and `.cc` under DIR, built with the firmware's flags and `-I DIR`; repeat it for more folders (not a folder holding `base/`) |
| `--ld SCRIPT` | your linker script (in `base/` or in a `--src` folder) |
| `--define NAME` | `-DNAME` for every source (yours and the base's) |
| `--leave-out FILE` | a base source left out (`firmware/src/...`), to replace it with your own |
| `--cflags DIR FLAGS` | FLAGS for the C files under DIR (a `--src` folder or a folder inside one), after the firmware's flags; the base's own files never get them |
| `--cxxflags DIR FLAGS` | the same for the C++ (`.cc`) files under DIR |
| `--asflags DIR FLAGS` | the same for the assembly (`.S`) files under DIR |

**Flags for your own folders.** Your code can have flags of its own, folder
by folder, while the base's files keep the base's (R-BUILD-5):

```sh
sh base/tools/build.sh build --out out --platform --src src --ld src/my.ld \
    --cflags src "-DMY_BOARD=2 -Wno-sign-compare" \
    --cflags src/vendor/dsp "-O2 -w -Iinclude" \
    --cxxflags src "-std=c++17"
```

- A file gets the flags of every folder it is under, in the order you
  gave them, after the firmware's own (so `-O2` here replaces the
  firmware's `-Os` for `src/vendor/dsp`, and its `-w` silences the
  warnings the firmware's `-Werror` would stop on).
- `--cflags` is for `.c` files only, `--cxxflags` for `.cc`, `--asflags`
  for `.S` (which are run through the preprocessor, so `-D` works there).
- A path in `-I`, `-isystem` or `-iquote` is from the folder the flags are
  for, and is joined to it: `-Iinclude`, not `-I include`.
- Taken: `-D`, `-U`, `-O`, `-W`, `-w`, `-f`, `-m`, `-std=`, `-I`,
  `-isystem`, `-iquote`, `-g`, `-pedantic`, `-ansi`, as words of letters,
  digits and `_ = + . , / : -`. Refused, so the build stays deterministic
  and inside its container: absolute paths and `..`, `-fdebug-prefix-map`
  and its kin, `-fprofile...`, `-fplugin...`, `-Wa,`, `-Wp,`, `-Wl,`,
  and anything else (`-o`, `-c`, `-x`, `-include`, `-target`, `@file`, ...).
- Your code is built for the SDK's CPU and float, whatever its flags:
  CPU r3, with the chip's single-precision float instructions (`fprev1`,
  as the base is built) or without float instructions (`-mno-fprev1`).
  Other `-m` flags are yours. The build reads each file's flags as the
  compiler does (its `-###` reading, the same the write-back check uses),
  so `-mcpu=`, `-mfprev2`, `-msimd`, a `-target-feature` and any flag
  with the same effect are all caught, and it stops before compiling any
  of your files, naming the folder, what the flag does and the fix:

  ```
  build: --cxxflags src: src/dsp/fir.cc would be built for double-precision float (fprev2), which the SDK's flags exclude and fwtest doesn't run (from -mfprev2).
  build:   Fix: take that out of --cxxflags src. Every --src folder is built for the SDK's CPU, r3, with its single-precision float (fprev1, as the base is) or without float instructions (-mno-fprev1); other -m flags are yours to set (BR-11; docs/BUILDING-ON-SMALL-BEEPS.md, section 5).
  FAIL: a folder's flags build for another CPU or other features than the SDK's (above)
  ```

  Refused alike: another CPU (`-mcpu=r4`, even `r3s`), SIMD (`-msimd`),
  and any other feature the toolchain has. fwtest
  runs what the SDK's flags give (R-HARN-14), not these.
- `--define NAME` stays the way to set something for every file, the
  base's included.

The outputs, in `out/`:

- `app.bin`: the raw image (linked at `0x02000000`), what fwtest and the
  app run;
- `app-pkg.bin`: the same code linked at `0x02000120`, for a `.fwsc`
  package (section 6);
- `app.elf`, `app-pkg.elf`: with symbols, for finding things;
- `app.size`: code, data, RAM and stack in bytes;
- `SHA256SUMS`.

The build is deterministic: the same sources give the same bytes, from
any folder on any machine. It refuses an object holding a store that
writes back into its own base register (`[++rN=k] = rN`, ...), as what
the chip does then is still open (R-BUILD-3); if your code trips it, the
message names the file, the function and the instruction. It reads each
object as it was compiled, with the CPU and float features your flags
gave it (`-mfprev1`, or a folder's own `-m` flags), and it refuses code
it can't read at all (`unreadable`), rather than guess past it.

  and why.

  be optimised. The guide's sizing section gives the figures as a table
  ("Where the store goes").

### 2026-10-29 clean-pin-flags: a folder's code for the SDK's CPU and float (amends BR-11, R-BUILD-5)

BR-11 let a `--src` folder set its own `-m` flags, so a folder could
build for another CPU or with instructions the SDK's flags leave out
(double-precision float, SIMD): code fwtest doesn't run (it runs the
forms `-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1` give, R-HARN-14).
The owner's rule: a folder may still set other `-m` flags, but its
objects are built for CPU `r3`, with the features `+fprev1` or none.

A relative path in `-I`, `-isystem` or `-iquote` is from DIR. Only `-D`, `-U`, `-O`, `-W`, `-w`, `-f`, `-m`, `-std=`, `-I`, `-isystem`, `-iquote`, `-g`, `-pedantic` and `-ansi` are taken, and of them not an absolute path or `..`, the prefix maps, `-fprofile`, `-fplugin`, `-fpass-plugin`, `-fsave-optimization-record`, `-Wa`, `-Wp`, `-Wl`; the outputs stay deterministic. ### 2026-10-29 clean-mllvm: the owner's answers on `-Xclang`, `-mllvm` and fwtest 0.10.0's counts (BR-11, R-BUILD-5)

clean-pin-flags left two questions on the flags a folder may set, and an
unexplained change in fwtest 0.10.0's instruction counts.

- **`-Xclang` stays refused.** As since clean-1028: it is not one of the
  families `check_flags` takes (exit 2).
- **`-mllvm` is refused outright.** It came in under `-m`, and passes
  options to the code generator past the driver, so the `-###` reading
  that keeps a folder's code to the SDK's CPU and float can't see what it
  does. `check_flags` now refuses `-mllvm` and its joined spelling
  `-mllvm=...` (exit 2) with a message saying why, before anything is
  built. Tested in C-UNIT (`FolderFlagsTest`: `-mllvm -fast-isel` and
  `-mllvm=-fast-isel` refused with the message, `-Xclang` still refused,
  plain `-m` flags taken) and among the flags case's refusals (C-SEAMS).
  The guide's section 5 says so.
- **fwtest 0.9.0 to 0.10.0: why three cases' counts moved.** The pin
  (#176) found audioload, store-busy and store-wipe's instruction counts
  per block differing in 28, 7 and 2 blocks (totals under 0.01 %), with
  every golden, outcome and check the same. The cause, from the spec
  side: 0.10.0 runs `*p &= ~m` on the same path as the other memory
  operations, which moves instruction counts slightly with the same
  results. These three cases are the ones that save while the audio
  runs.
EOF
echo ok

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.
